A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SWE-fficiency benchmark of 498 tasks across nine repositories. Their main text, tables, figures, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent evaluations, patch-outcome measurements, localization analyses, and comparisons of manually annotated and LM-generated workloads.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations, adds results for four models, and reports an additional repeated-measurement study in Appendix N.

M1.justification: The optimization task, agent prompts, collection framework, and reward-hacking defenses are retained. Expanded descriptions of test-selection tooling and annotation do not establish an actual procedural change. Both stack-frame checking and process-isolated timing already appear in v1 Appendix J.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 498-task, nine-repository benchmark and retain the 100-task SWE-fficiency Lite subset. No additional evaluated domain, task requirement, or input scenario is established.

E2.justification: Tables 2, 3, 6, and 7 expand the OpenHands comparison from 11 to 15 models by adding Claude 4.5 Opus, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, and Gemini 3 Pro. Existing models and the three SWE-agent comparisons remain, substantially extending the frontier-model comparison.

E3.justification: Section 2.3 changes the primary benchmark scoring rule: v3 floors each speedup ratio at 0.001 before harmonic aggregation and similarly clamps failed or empty patches' fallback scores. v1 specifies no such floor. This changes how extreme poor outcomes influence the headline metric; hardware, action budgets, and Lite sampling remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a small fixed-patch measurement-stability study in Appendix N, covering-test distribution analysis in Appendix E.3, and illustrative workload-tradeoff cases in Appendix D. Existing difficulty, localization, workload-generation, and patch-example analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 11 newly reports three independent evaluations of patches from three selected agents and the expert, including individual SR measurements and their spreads. v1 already reports workload means, standard deviations, and filtering thresholds. This adds measurement-repeatability reporting, not repeated model-generation trials or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Tables 2/6 add Claude 4.5 Opus at 0.225× and revise many existing scores, including Claude 4.5 Sonnet from 0.041× to 0.116× and Claude 3.7 Sonnet from 0.047× to 0.024×. Table 8 reverses Gemini Pro/Flash SR ordering from 0.001/0.002 to 0.008/0.007 and changes correctness rates. Patch outcomes and new stability results also change. Revised scoring prevents interpreting these as clean same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The SR definition gains a mathematical lower bound and the failed-patch rule becomes max(1/Speedup_gold, 0.001). Otherwise, the profiling definitions, greedy attribution procedure, and coverage/loss equations match between v1 Appendix G and v3 Appendix I; no new proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract's reported expert-performance bound changes from below 0.15× to below 0.23×. The introduction explicitly frames targeted workload optimization as a foundational capability preceding broader production performance engineering. The benchmark, collection pipeline, and central claim of a substantial expert gap remain.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands validity and applicability discussion. Appendix D explains accepted tradeoffs across workloads; Appendix K qualifies manual-versus-LM superiority because humans received additional PR context and only Gemini 2.5 Flash was tested. It also adds multi-objective limitations, a patch-size interpretation, and claims that measurement stability supports reliable rankings.

D1.justification: v3 documents symbol resolution, coverage cleanup, and the detailed test-selection toolchain; annotator calibration, peer verification, approximately 200 author-hours, and a workload template; and the policy of preserving expert-specific warmup behavior. The HuggingFace dataset identifier changes from swefficiency-anon/swefficiency to swefficiency/swefficiency. These substantial disclosures improve implementation transparency, although exact harness version identifiers from v1 are omitted.

R1.justification: v3 removes the foundational optimization/synthesis paragraph and its citations, drops model-announcement references, and adds Liu et al. (2024) for measurement variability. It sharpens the library-maintainer perspective relative to function-level benchmarks while retaining the central positioning against GSO and SWE-Perf.

P1.justification: Most section order and existing prose remain, with targeted explanatory rewrites. The Ethics Statement becomes an expanded Impact Statement, a conflict-of-interest disclosure is added, and the standalone Reproducibility Statement is removed. New appendix sections are inserted and subsequent sections renumbered.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout, substantially relocating and resizing displays; Tables 2 and 3 become adjacent. v3 adds annotation-template Figure 15 and stability Table 11 and expands model tables. Existing plots and code-diff examples are retained rather than replaced with new analyses.

improvement.justification: v3 improves reproducibility through concrete curation details and corrects an important interpretive weakness by acknowledging unequal information in the manual-versus-LM workload comparison. Broader model comparisons and better agreement between Tables 3 and 7 also help. Benefits are limited by unresolved reporting inconsistencies: Table 11 gives Claude 3.7 SR near 0.048 versus 0.024 in Table 2, and Section 4.1 retains outdated scores and exceptions. The net improvement is modest.
